\section[\texorpdfstring{\te{చెల్లించు} (celliñcu)}{చెల్లించు (celliñcu)}]{\te{చెల్లించు} (celliñcu) — to pay}

\label{lesson:TE-C157-cellincu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Telugu for an advertisement, then the Telugu for a receipt.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{చెల్లించు}}
\textbf{\te{చెల్లించు}} — \emph{celliñcu} — \textquotedblleft{}to pay\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{చెల్లించు}} (\emph{celliñcu}) is native Dravidian, made from \emph{cellu}, \textquotedblleft{}to pass, be current, be paid\textquotedblright{} (DEDR 2781). Malayalam \emph{celuttuka}, \textquotedblleft{}to pay\textquotedblright{}, stands in the same entry.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{celliñcu}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{celliñcu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Telugu for an advertisement, then the Telugu for a receipt, then say \emph{celliñcu} again
\end{itemize}

Before the new one: say the Telugu for a receipt, then the Telugu for to pay.

\textbf{\te{వేయించు}} — \emph{vēyiñcu} — \textquotedblleft{}to fry, to roast\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{వేయించు}} (\emph{vēyiñcu}) is native Dravidian. DEDR 5517 lists nasalised forms of \emph{vēgiñcu} and \emph{vēpu}, \textquotedblleft{}to fry, grill\textquotedblright{}, with Tamil \emph{vē}, \textquotedblleft{}to burn, be boiled, cooked\textquotedblright{}, and Kannada \emph{bēyu}, \textquotedblleft{}to be cooked\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\textbf{\te{కలుపు}} (\emph{kalupu}) is native Dravidian. DEDR 1299 gives it as \emph{kalapu}, \textquotedblleft{}to mix, join\textquotedblright{}, with Tamil \emph{kala} and Kannada \emph{kalasu}, \textquotedblleft{}to mix\textquotedblright{}. DEDR compares Sanskrit \emph{kalka}, \textquotedblleft{}a paste\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 2939).

\section[\texorpdfstring{\te{రుబ్బు} (rubbu)}{రుబ్బు (rubbu)}]{\te{రుబ్బు} (rubbu) — to grind (wet batter)}

\label{lesson:TE-C157-rubbu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Telugu for to boil, then the Telugu for to mix.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{రుబ్బు}}
\textbf{\te{రుబ్బు}} — \emph{rubbu} — \textquotedblleft{}to grind (wet batter)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{రుబ్బు}} (\emph{rubbu}) is native Dravidian. DEDR 665 lists \emph{rubbu}, \textquotedblleft{}to grind in a mortar\textquotedblright{}, with Tamil \emph{urai}, \textquotedblleft{}to rub into a paste\textquotedblright{}, and Kannada \emph{ujju}, \textquotedblleft{}to rub\textquotedblright{}. DEDR compares, with a query, Sanskrit \emph{uñchati}, \textquotedblleft{}gleans\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 1680).
\end{cousinweb}
